query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If an otherwise conventional eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high–entropy alloy (HEA) is processed by a hybrid thermo‐mechanical route—specifically, by severe cryogenic rolling followed by warm rolling—it will develop a hierarchically refined duplex lamellar microstructure containing both retained coarse lamellae and interspersed nanocrystalline regions. This refined structure will exhibit a higher density of beneficial (e.g., serrated) phase boundaries that delay microcrack initiation and propagation, thereby simultaneously improving both room‑temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the as‐cast, coarse‐lamellar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA featuring dual‐phase (L12 and B2) lamellar colonies with relatively coarse spacing and straight internal boundaries that are prone to microcracking.
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid thermo‐mechanical processing route that consists of cryogenic rolling (to impart severe plastic deformation at low temperature) followed immediately by warm rolling (e.g., near 600°C) to promote controlled recovery and refinement.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed under controlled rolling conditions—cryogenic deformation in incremental strain steps at cryogenic temperature, followed by warm rolling at an established warm temperature (around 600°C). Tensile tests are performed at room temperature under standardized strain rates; additional microstructural characterization (TEM, EBSD) is used to assess lamellar spacing and interface morphology.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically refined duplex microstructure in which the original coarse lamellae become subdivided into ultrafine lamellae and interspersed nanocrystalline regions, with improved and possibly serrated phase boundaries that impede crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The severe deformation followed by a controlled warm deformation stage produces a multi‐scale microstructure that increases the density of interfaces. These interfaces provide enhanced back stress and strain hardening by promoting load partitioning between stiffer and softer regions. Furthermore, the modified (e.g., serrated) phase boundaries effectively blunt and arrest microcrack propagation, overcoming the intrinsic weakness of the as‐cast lamellar boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as‐cast lamellar HEA, the hybrid processed alloy is expected to show both an increased tensile yield strength and enhanced room‐temperature ductility. Although the exact magnitudes depend on processing details, a significant improvement in the strength–ductility synergy is anticipated.
generation.baseline: As‐cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with coarse, straight lamellar colonies in which phase boundaries often act as sites for microcrack initiation under room‐temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The intervention is valid provided the processing parameters (cryogenic deformation strain, warm rolling temperature near 600°C, and subsequent stabilization) remain in the regimes typical for the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and that testing is carried out under standard room‐temperature tensile conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on the detailed processing parameters (e.g., strain rate, total imposed strain, and exact warm rolling temperature), which require further optimization. Thus, the magnitude of the improvement is uncertain at this stage.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA samples: one set left in the as‐cast condition (baseline) and the other subjected to the hybrid processing (cryo-rolling followed by warm rolling at ~600°C). Characterize their microstructures using TEM and EBSD to verify the formation of the refined hierarchical duplex lamellar structure with modified interfaces. Subsequently, perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to compare tensile yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and grain size (via TEM/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid processed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the as-cast baseline, or if the targeted hierarchical duplex microstructure with refined or serrated phase boundaries is not confirmed by microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Given the energy-efficient improvement and large safety factors, the attainment of high strength and high ductility in materials is arguably a vital requirement for most engineering applications. Unfortunately, these two properties are generally mutually exclusive, particularly in pure metals and alloys. Eutectic alloys specifically exhibit good liquidity and castability, preventing common casting flaws, like internal shrinkage and compositional segregation, to downgrade mechanical properties. They also possess a regularly arranged lamellar organization that can be viewed as a natural or in situ composite, which enables synergetic reinforcement to improve mechanical properties and sometimes bring unusual electrical, magnetic, and optical behaviors. Eutectic materials have therefore been investigated in diverse application fields, but traditionally, only certain eutectic systems have been of major commercial importance. Recently, eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), first proposed by Lu et al. in 2014, were designed based on the above eutectic-alloy concept. A commonly adopted strategy to overcome this strength-ductility tradeoff is to develop multi-phase microstructures, involving at least one ductile/soft and one hard/strong phase, mixed in the appropriate proportion. Common examples include duplex alloys, such as 2205 stainless steel, which have a hard bcc phase to increase the strength of the alloy and a soft fcc phase to maintain the tensile ductility while deformation. The goal has been on fine-tuning the alloy composition and/or processing conditions in order to obtain a material with a good balance between ductility and strength. Eutectic alloys, often exhibiting a two-phase lamellar microstructure, offer such a possibility, and have been investigated for many years in different classes of alloys. Eutectic morphologies are characterized by the simultaneous growth of two (or more) phases from the liquid. A recently developed new class of eutectic HEAs (EHEAs), have attracted a lot of attention due to their promising mechanical properties.
